LLMRcontent treats model labels as measured variables. A study defines the
instrument, develops candidate protocols on designated rows, validates one
locked protocol against held-out human labels, and carries the remaining
classification error into corpus estimates. Robustness checks show how
specified measurement choices affect the estimand, while replication archives
connect results to recorded calls.

```{r}
library(LLMRcontent)
```

## Coding with held-out validation

The codebook states the construct and its category boundaries.

```{r}
cb <- codebook(
  name = "policy appraisal",
  unit = "one statement",
  categories = list(
    cb_category("supportive", "Presents the proposal as beneficial."),
    cb_category("critical", "Presents the proposal as harmful or deficient.")
  ),
  version = "1.0"
)

cb
```

The study begins with a finite corpus: every statement whose category shares
it will report, each with a stable identifier. In this simulated corpus a fifth
of the statements are worded ambiguously, and the vector `truth` stands in for
the judgment of a trained human coder. It labels the statements drawn for the
audit, and at the end it gives the share the estimates are meant to recover.

```{r}
set.seed(110)
n <- 120
truth <- sample(c("supportive", "critical"), n, replace = TRUE,
                prob = c(0.4, 0.6))
wording <- ifelse(truth == "supportive", "clear public benefit",
                  "serious public harm")
wording[sample(n, 24)] <- "mixed evidence"
corpus <- data.frame(
  id = sprintf("s%03d", seq_len(n)),
  text = paste(wording, "in statement", seq_len(n)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
```

The audited statements are a simple random sample of the corpus, and human
coders label them. Before labels are collected, `gold_size()` can compare
candidate sample sizes for a target width of the agreement interval.

```{r}
audited <- sample(nrow(corpus), 40)
gold_data <- data.frame(
  corpus[audited, c("id", "text")],
  label = truth[audited],
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
```

The gold set divides the audited statements into a development split, used to
choose a protocol, and a test split, which is sealed for evaluating the chosen
one. By default `gold_set()` stratifies the split by label, so that both splits
have the same class composition. That suits validation. A split stratified by
the human label is close to a simple random sample of the corpus, but not
exactly one: rounding the allocation within each label gives statements of
different labels slightly different chances of entering the test split. With
`stratify = FALSE` the test split is a simple random sample of the audited
statements, and therefore of the corpus, which is what the correction below
asserts.

```{r}
gold <- gold_set(
  gold_data,
  text = "text",
  label = "label",
  id = "id",
  split = c(dev = 0.5, test = 0.5),
  stratify = FALSE
)

gold
```

Execution functions accept a `.runner`, a function that receives request rows
and returns them with a `response_text` column. This offline response function
labels by keyword without contacting a provider. It codes every ambiguous
statement as critical, except under a prompt that ends with "Label:", where it
codes them as supportive.

```{r}
offline_coder <- function(requests, ...) {
  prompt <- vapply(requests$messages, `[[`, "", "user")
  requests$response_text <- ifelse(
    grepl("benefit", requests$text, fixed = TRUE), "supportive", "critical"
  )
  ambiguous <- grepl("mixed evidence", requests$text, fixed = TRUE)
  requests$response_text[ambiguous & grepl("Label:$", prompt)] <- "supportive"
  requests
}
```

Candidate protocols are compared on the development split. The tuning table is
sorted by accuracy, and its `protocol_id` column gives each candidate's position
in the list, which selects the winner whatever its label. Locking the winner
fixes its hash over the codebook, prompt, model configuration, and parser; the
same locked object is used for validation and for coding the corpus.

```{r}
cfg <- LLMR::llm_config("groq", "offline-demo", temperature = 0)
candidates <- list(
  protocol(cb, cfg, label = "full codebook"),
  protocol(cb, cfg, prompt = "{codebook}\n\n{text}\nLabel:", label = "terse")
)

tuning <- tune_protocol(candidates, gold, .runner = offline_coder)
tuning$table[c("protocol", "protocol_id", "accuracy", "acc_lo", "acc_hi")]

locked <- protocol_lock(candidates[[tuning$table$protocol_id[[1]]]])
locked
```

The locked protocol is evaluated once on the sealed test split, and the
evaluation is recorded in the gold-set ledger.

```{r}
validation <- validate_protocol(
  locked,
  gold,
  .runner = offline_coder
)

validation
```

The validation result reports holdout accuracy, its exact interval,
category-level performance, and parse failures. These quantities describe
agreement with the human labels. They do not establish that the codebook
captures the construct.

The same protocol then codes the whole corpus, audited statements included.

```{r}
coded <- code_corpus(
  corpus,
  locked,
  "text",
  id = "id",
  .runner = offline_coder
)

coded_data <- tibble::as_tibble(coded)
head(coded_data[c("id", "label")])
```

`gold_correct()` pairs the human and model labels of the test-split statements,
which it finds in the coded corpus by `id`. For each category, the corrected
share is the corpus share of model labels in that category plus the mean, over
the audited pairs, of the difference between the human indicator and the model
indicator for the category. This is the difference estimator of survey
sampling. Its standard error is `sqrt((1 - n/N) * s2 / n)`, where `s2` is the
variance of the paired differences, `n` the number of pairs, and `N` the number
of coded statements with a parsed label; the corpus share adds no sampling
error, because the
corpus is the population whose shares are estimated. When model and human
labels mostly agree, the differences vary little, and the corrected share is
more precise than the share of human labels among the audited statements alone.

The estimator and its standard error assume that the audited statements are a
simple random sample of the coded corpus, so the call requires that assertion:
`design = "srs"` states it, and the default refuses to compute a correction
from an undeclared audit.

```{r}
corrected <- gold_correct(coded, gold, design = "srs")

corrected
mean(truth == "supportive")
```

The model codes every ambiguous statement as critical, so the naive supportive
share falls below the simulated share of 0.40. The interval for the corrected
share covers 0.40, but with 20 audited pairs the point estimate is noisy: here
it lies above the simulated share by about as much as the naive share lies
below it. The development statements that chose the protocol are part of the
corpus as well, while the test split is a random sample of the rest of it.
Because the protocol was chosen for its accuracy on the development
statements, the correction can understate the model's error among them, by an
amount that shrinks with their share of the corpus. Interpretation remains
conditional on the codebook and the human labels.

`LLMR::report()` combines the validation result with the locked protocol and
gold set. The report includes the holdout ledger, which now records the
validation and correction.

```{r}
methods <- LLMR::report(
  validation,
  gold = gold,
  protocol = locked
)

methods
```

## Robustness and replication

A robustness audit recomputes an estimand across prompt wording, label order,
and temperature. Here the estimand is the supportive share centered at 0.5.

```{r}
plan <- audit_plan(
  data = corpus,
  text = "text",
  estimator = function(d) {
    mean(d$label == "supportive", na.rm = TRUE) - 0.5
  },
  labels = c("supportive", "critical"),
  prompt = paste(
    "Classify as one of: {labels}.",
    "",
    "{text}",
    "",
    "Label:",
    sep = "\n"
  )
)

plan <- audit_add_models(plan, list(keyword = cfg))
plan <- audit_add_prompts(
  plan,
  concise = "Choose one label from {labels} for this statement: {text}"
)
plan <- audit_add_perturbations(
  plan,
  label_order = "reversed",
  temperature = 0.7
)

audit <- audit_run(plan, .runner = offline_coder)

audit_stability(audit)
audit_fragility(audit)
```

`audit_stability()` describes variation inside the specified grid, not across
all possible measurement choices. `audit_fragility()` measures the smallest
number of changed grid dimensions needed to alter the stated conclusion. Here
the concise prompt moves the ambiguous statements from supportive to critical,
and the estimate moves with it; a substantive study should include defensible
prompt and model alternatives.

The offline response function writes no LLMR call log, so one compact JSON
record supplies the fields needed to demonstrate archive construction.

```{r}
log_path <- tempfile(fileext = ".jsonl")
writeLines(paste0(
  '{"ts":"2026-07-01T10:00:01+0000","schema_version":"1.0","kind":"call",',
  '"provider":"groq","model":"offline-demo","status":200,',
  '"request":{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Classify statement 1"}],',
  '"temperature":0},"usage":{"sent":12,"rec":1},',
  '"response_id":"offline-1","text":"supportive"}'
), log_path)

archive <- archive_seal(
  archive_build(log_path, name = "offline-study")
)

archive_check(
  archive,
  results = data.frame(response_id = "offline-1")
)
```

The check compares the stored record with its content hash and seal, then
matches the result identifier to the logged call. A successful check establishes
integrity and linkage; it does not promise the same reply from a changed model
or provider.

`archive_write()` stores the records and manifest in a directory. After
`archive_read()`, `archive_check()` verifies the copy and `LLMR::report()`
summarizes it.

```{r}
archive_dir <- tempfile("offline-study-")
archive_write(archive, archive_dir)

copy <- archive_read(archive_dir)
archive_check(copy)
LLMR::report(copy)
```
